the category of promotional item or refreshment that may lawfully be offered without becoming an enrollment inducement, bounded by a value limit set in current-year rules and never conditioned on enrolling; meals at sales events sit outside this class entirely

the standing practice of comparing the federal, state, carrier and upline layers that govern an activity, following the strictest reading rather than the most convenient source, and recording which layers were compared and why

the pre-approval step every prospecting, marketing, event, partnership or retention idea passes through - one paragraph naming its rule class, the permission or approval artifact it will leave behind, and a named approver - where an idea that cannot produce an artifact does not run

a named category of period during which a beneficiary may make a specific kind of coverage election; each class differs in who qualifies, what change is allowed and when the resulting coverage begins, and each is verified per case against a current plan-year official source

the window class opening around a person's first eligibility, anchored to their eligibility event rather than to the calendar; it is the one time most beneficiaries can enter any coverage route with the fewest conditions attached

the recurring fall window in which most beneficiaries may change plans for the following coverage year; it concentrates the year's plan-change work into a few weeks and creates the practice's seasonal capacity problem

a window class opened by a documented qualifying event - a permanent move out of a service area, loss of employer or other creditable coverage, a plan contract change, a change in assistance status - whose qualification must be evidenced rather than assumed

prior coverage the rules treat as good enough to avoid a late-enrollment charge for the relevant program part; whether a given plan counts is determined by that plan's own creditable-coverage notice and the current rules, never by the agent's judgment

the mechanism that prices uncovered months - a surcharge derived from the number of months without creditable coverage, attached to premium and lasting for a period the current rules define; the defense against it is the plan's creditable-coverage notice held in the file, and its amount is verified in current-year sources rather than stated from memory

a limited period or triggering situation in which a supplement carrier must issue a policy without medical underwriting; outside it most states allow underwriting, which is what makes leaving the supplement route a decision that may not be reversible on the same terms

the two dominant mechanisms compared in this business - the original-program-plus-supplement route with separate drug coverage, access following program participation and cost concentrated in predictable premium, and the all-in-one advantage-class route with a private network, point-of-service cost-sharing and an annual out-of-pocket ceiling - explained as mechanisms rather than as brands or verdicts

the list stating whether a plan covers a drug, at what cost tier and under what conditions such as prior authorization, step therapy or quantity limits, all set per plan and per coverage year and checked against the client's actual medication list rather than assumed

an annual ceiling on a member's cost-sharing that exists in some coverage architectures and not in others; its presence or absence is the clearest way to describe worst-case exposure without quoting a number
the client's current arrangement carried into the comparison as an explicit option, so that changing plans must earn its place against staying put rather than being assumed

a provider, facility or medication the client has stated they will not give up, recorded in writing at intake and ranked before any plan is named, so a later failure to satisfy it is visible rather than quietly traded away

the structural control against the bias this business carries - criteria fixed in writing before any candidate set exists, at least one non-maximizing option shown, the do-nothing baseline retained, the member-side reason recorded for stays as rigorously as for moves, and book skew audited - so that compensation cannot enter a recommendation in either direction

the first-class operating standard owed to a protected population: consented channels and humane hours, plain language, pace set by the beneficiary, comprehension checked by restatement, a trusted person of their own choosing offered and recorded, no urgency or loss framing, an immediate and permanent stop on request, and a documented hard stop where capacity, comprehension or signing authority is in doubt

the dated written capture made before any plan is named - the medication list exactly as taken with strength and quantity, the providers and facilities ranked must-keep or nice-to-keep in the client's own words, utilization-predicting conditions captured operationally, travel and pharmacy patterns, and the client's own risk tolerance - that the entire comparison is later defended against

the payment class that continues on a member who stays enrolled beyond the initial payment period, as distinct from the payment for a first-time enrollment; its existence, level and duration are set by the applicable regulated schedule and carrier contract and are verified per plan year rather than remembered

the per-member determination of which payment level applies, derived from that member's own enrollment history - new to the product class, continuously enrolled, moving between plans in a way the rules treat as preserving the level, or returning after a gap - and never surfaced in member-facing material

the carrier-side attribute recording which appointed agent is credited with and paid on a given member; it is set by the accepted enrollment and can move when the member enrolls through another agent, a carrier's own line or a public channel, and servicing someone loyally neither creates nor restores it

an enrolled member with no active agent of record, typically because the writing agent left, lost the appointment or was terminated; orphans may be assigned or may simply call whoever answers, and servicing one is legitimate work that must never be conditioned on an attribution change

the reversal of compensation already paid, triggered by mechanisms such as an early disenrollment inside the period the rules define for recovery, a retroactive termination for non-payment or lost eligibility, a reversed enrollment after a complaint, or a reclassified payment level; the exposure is created upstream by enrollment quality

the yearly notice a plan sends its members describing what changes for the coming plan year in cost sharing, formulary, network and benefits; it is the trigger document for the annual review cycle and the first thing an agent reads before contacting that member

the pattern of members staying enrolled and attributed over time, read as a diagnostic rather than a target: high persistency usually indicates fit quality and responsive service, while a drop points at a specific upstream cause class to fix

a contact whose purpose is helping a member use the coverage they already hold - a card, a bill, a pharmacy rejection, a provider question - which becomes a marketing or sales contact the moment a different plan or a new election enters the conversation, at which point the required permission and scope artifacts must exist before anything further is said

the set of members on whom the agent holds an agent-of-record position across carriers together with the servicing relationships around them; it is held under carrier and upline contract terms - release, assignment, vesting-class treatment of renewals, post-termination payment, transferability - rather than owned outright

the free, unbiased counseling channel available to beneficiaries in each state; it is a legitimate referral destination whenever a member needs help the agent may not give, including appeal representation and comparison assistance with no agent interest attached

the single definition of a complete prospect or client file - permission artifact and source, scope agreement, materials presented with approval identifiers and plan-year versions, the needs discussion and the beneficiary's own stated reasons in their own words, disclosures, accommodations offered, ready-to-sell evidence for the product written, and the submission confirmation - built at the time of the conversation and passing a retrieval drill inside the shortest applicable response window

competency_questions_covered: Which credentials, certifications and contracts must be in force before I may market or enroll anyone this plan year, and how do I verify each is actually current rather than assumed current?
How do I decide whether a growth idea is allowed at all, and what do I do when no compliant version of it exists?
What does the annual certification cycle actually require, in what order should I complete it, and what happens to my season if I miss a carrier's window?
How should I structure my carrier contracts and my upline hierarchy, and what will it cost me to move a contract later?
When may I contact a prospect at all, what counts as permission, which regime does it come from, and how long does it last?
What must be agreed and documented before a personal appointment, and what may and may not be discussed once I am in the room?
Which marketing practices are flatly prohibited and which are permitted only with conditions attached?
Before any flyer, page, post or advertisement goes public, what review, disclosure and versioning does it need?
How do I run an educational or a sales event without turning presence-building into a violation?
How do I buy or generate leads without inheriting somebody else's compliance failure, and how do I keep one channel from being able to end my season?
What extra care do I owe an older, grieving or impaired prospect, who may sign, and when must I stop the conversation entirely?
What exactly must be in a prospect or client file, how is health and identity data handled, and how fast can I produce a complete file on request?
What do I do on the day a complaint, a secret-shop finding or a carrier investigation lands on me?
How do I keep the whole compliance stack current as rules, carriers and my own footprint change from one plan year to the next?
Which enrollment window is this person actually in right now, what change does it allow, and when would that change take effect?
What has to be true before I am allowed to have this conversation at all, and what exactly am I telling the client I am and am not doing?
What must I know about this person before any plan name is spoken, and how do I capture it so a later recommendation is defensible as need-driven?
What coverage does this person already hold, what happens to it if they enroll, and where is the gap that creates a late-enrollment charge?
How do I find out whether this client qualifies for assistance that changes both what they should buy and which windows they have, without prejudging them?
How do the two main coverage architectures actually work, and which parts of that choice are hard to undo later?
How do I check this client's own doctors and prescriptions against a candidate plan without turning a directory entry into a promise?
How do I show what a plan will really cost this person over a year without inventing numbers or reducing it to the lowest premium?
How do I keep the shortlist honestly driven by this client's needs when the options do not all pay me the same?
How do I run the meeting so the beneficiary genuinely makes the decision, including when a family member is pushing or the client is struggling to follow?
What has to be right at submission, and how do I confirm the person is actually covered on the date they think they are?
What file must exist afterward so a third party could reconstruct this enrollment a year later, and what is handed to the service side?
What do I do when the calendar has already gone wrong - a missed window, a weak special-window claim, or an election that produced the wrong result?
How do I get through the annual window without letting volume degrade the quality of any single enrollment?
What actually keeps a payment coming on a member I already enrolled, and how do I verify that for this plan year instead of trusting last year's understanding?
A plan change is clearly better for this member but it costs me compensation or triggers a recoupment - how do I decide, and what has to be in the file afterward?
How do I know whether I am still the agent of record on a member, and what do I do when I find out I am not?
A carrier statement does not match the members I believe I have - how do I find the gap, dispute it with evidence, and how should the timing of this income shape my planning?
A client calls in the middle of the year because a specialist has left the network - what is the correct sequence of steps?
A client's drug cost jumped at the pharmacy counter - how do I work out which mechanism produced it and what legitimate help exists?
A claim was denied or an unexpected bill arrived - how far can I help before I am acting outside my role?
At what exact point does a service call become a marketing or sales contact, and what has to exist before it goes any further?
How do I run an annual review that is genuinely need-driven, fits inside the contact rules, and treats 'nothing needs to change' as a complete outcome?
Which clients should I contact proactively and how often, and how does that change when a member is impaired or a family member starts speaking for them?
What life events in a member's circumstances do I need to notice, and what do I do with one when I find it?
My book lost more members than usual this year - how do I read that, and which of my own practices does it tell me to change?
How do I grow from a satisfied book by referral without breaking contact rules or inducement rules?
What do I actually hold when I call this book mine, and what happens to these members if I move upline, lose an appointment or stop practicing?
